strengths: The paper identifies a real and well-motivated problem: reparameterization policy gradients (RPG) remain unstable even with modern variance reduction (SHAC/SAPO), as evidenced by the KL-spike analysis in Figure 1.

The core technical idea—establishing the connection between the PPO surrogate objective and reparameterization gradients via BPTT, with cached action-gradients, noise regeneration (Eq. 12), and importance-weighted off-policy reuse (Eq. 13)—is sensible, clearly described, and non-obvious.

Experiments are reasonably thorough: five tasks across two differentiable simulators (DFlex, Rewarped), 12 random seeds, three baselines (PPO, SHAC, SAPO), deterministic and stochastic final evaluations, and component-wise ablations (Figure 5, Table 2).

The authors show commendable attention to baseline fairness: Appendix C.3 ablates giving SAPO the same exponential learning-rate schedule and the same number of critic update epochs, demonstrating RPO's gains are not merely due to those hyperparameter changes.

Hyperparameters, architectures, and implementation details (including subtleties about entropy gradient treatment and squashed-Gaussian KL computation) are documented in Appendix C, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical treatment is thin. The central claim that Equation (13) is the gradient of the clipped surrogate objective (Equation 8) is asserted rather than derived or proven; Appendix D is informal. Issues such as unbiasedness of the single-sample Monte Carlo Q estimate, the bias introduced by truncated-horizon BPTT with a bootstrapped value function, and gradient behavior at clipping boundaries deserve formal statement.

The claimed novelty is modest: the method is essentially PPO's clipped objective plus KL regularization transplanted to RPG with short-horizon BPTT (i.e., SHAC as the base estimator). The delta over GI-PPO (which also does PPO-style updates for RPG-related methods) and over SAPO is incremental, and a head-to-head with GI-PPO is absent.

The evidence for component claims is weaker than the rhetoric. Table 2 ablation gaps are small relative to reported standard deviations (e.g., RPO 9035±266 vs. no-KL 8983±403), and no statistical significance tests are reported; the text's 'significantly degraded' language is not supported quantitatively. Ablations are performed only on Humanoid.

Computational cost is not addressed. Reusing samples over M=5 epochs and caching per-action gradients incurs extra compute and memory; sample efficiency is reported only in environment steps, with no wall-clock or memory comparison against SHAC/SAPO, which matters for differentiable-simulation methods whose appeal is speed.

Limitations discussion is missing. There is no treatment of when the method applies (requires fully differentiable dynamics), gradient explosion through contact-rich dynamics, sensitivity to the asymmetric clipping constants, or the sim-to-real gap other than a one-line future-work mention.

Presentation/reference issues: references [28] and [29] are the same paper cited twice under different numbers (Rewarped is cited inconsistently as [28] and [29]); several URLs in Appendix A are blank; Figure 2/3 are schematic and could be more informative.
No code release is stated, which limits reproducibility of a method with several non-trivial implementation details (noise regeneration, entropy gradient handling, LR schedules).

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: RPG methods (SHAC, SAPO) in differentiable simulation still suffer from destabilizing policy updates, and the motivating Figure 1 (KL spikes coinciding with performance drops in Humanoid) convincingly establishes the gap.

The idea of connecting the PPO clipped surrogate objective to reparameterization policy gradients, and using cached action-gradients plus BPTT to enable multiple epochs of stable sample reuse, is a sensible and relatively unexplored direction that could be broadly useful for differentiable-simulation RL.

Experiments are reasonably thorough: five locomotion/manipulation tasks across two simulators, 12 seeds per run, comparison to SAPO, SHAC, and PPO with shared implementations and aligned hyperparameters, plus deterministic and stochastic evaluation protocols.

An ablation study (Section 6.3, Tables 2 and 5, Figure 5) isolates the contributions of KL regularization, sample reuse epochs, and clipping, and Appendix C.3 reports additional fairness checks (exponential LR schedule and critic-epoch-matched SAPO baselines), which shows good experimental hygiene.
Hyperparameters and implementation details are documented in appendices, including environment counts and RPO-specific coefficients, supporting reasonable reproducibility.
weaknesses: A central soundness concern: the paper claims (Sections 4 and 5, Appendix D) that the off-policy reparameterization gradient, ρ(θ')∇_θa∇_aR(τ), is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the reparameterization gradient of the importance-weighted surrogate objective. This appears to be incorrect: differentiating E[ρ(θ)A(s, f_θ(ε))] with respect to θ requires the product rule and yields an additional term involving ∇_θρ(θ)·A that is dropped in Equation (13). No proof is provided that this term vanishes, and the derivation in Appendix D asserts unbiasedness without justification. For a paper whose headline contribution is the 'connection' between RPG and the PPO surrogate, this theoretical gap is material.

The asymmetric, advantage-sign-independent clipping in Equation (8) is motivated qualitatively ('RPG, unlike REINFORCE, does not explicitly increase or decrease action probabilities') but its gradient consequence (Equation 13 hard-zeros contributions outside the clipping range) further deviates from the gradient of any well-defined objective. The estimator is thus a heuristic whose formal properties (bias, consistency, relation to a trust region) are not analyzed; claims of a 'principled way to enable stable sample reuse' are stronger than what is established.

Ablation results are overstated relative to the evidence: Table 2 shows final Humanoid performance of 8983±403 (no KL), 8740±477 (no clipping), and 8329±404 (2 epochs) versus 9035±266 for full RPO—differences that largely overlap within one standard deviation—yet the text concludes each component is necessary and training is 'significantly' degraded. Ablations are also run on only one task (Humanoid), limiting generality.

The empirical gains over the strongest baseline (SAPO) are modest on some tasks: Hopper and Hand Reorient are essentially on par in Table 1, and improvements elsewhere, while real, are moderate. The wall-clock cost of RPO (BPTT gradient caching plus five policy epochs with action regeneration) is never reported, so 'superior sample efficiency' may come at unquantified compute cost.

Baselines are incomplete: GI-PPO [23] is discussed in Related Work as the most directly related hybrid (RPG + PPO-style off-policy updates), yet it is excluded from experiments on the grounds of prior reported results rather than being re-run under the paper's shared setup.

Presentation and referencing issues: references [28] and [29] are the same paper cited twice; some environment and repository details in Appendices A and C rely on links that do not render in the text; no code release is stated, which weakens reproducibility of a method with many implementation-sensitive components (action regeneration, noise recovery in Equation 12, entropy gradient handling described only informally in C.2).

The method assumes Gaussian policies with invertible reparameterization transforms (Equation 12) and smooth differentiable dynamics; limitations regarding non-smooth/contact dynamics, long horizons, and learned world models—precisely the settings where RPG is hardest—are acknowledged only implicitly and not tested.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: the paper empirically demonstrates (Figure 1) that even state-of-the-art RPG methods (SHAC, SAPO) suffer from large policy updates and performance collapses, motivating an explicit trust-region-like mechanism for reparameterization gradients.

The core technical insight is genuinely useful and non-trivial: connecting the PPO-style surrogate objective to reparameterization gradients via BPTT, with a practical mechanism (caching action-gradients once per trajectory, regenerating actions by recovering the noise epsilon, and importance-weighting for off-policy updates) that enables sample reuse at low overhead (single backward pass per trajectory).

The clipped surrogate (Eq. 8) and gradient form (Eq. 13) are sensibly adapted to the RPG setting: asymmetric clipping independent of the advantage sign is a reasonable design given that RPG does not explicitly reweight action probabilities the way REINFORCE does, and the decision to add explicit KL regularization (and showing clipping alone is insufficient) is empirically grounded via the ablation.

Solid empirical evaluation: 12 random seeds per experiment, two differentiable simulators (DFlex, Rewarped), five tasks spanning locomotion and manipulation, both deterministic and stochastic evaluation protocols, and comparisons against strong baselines (SHAC with the improved SAPO-repository implementation, SAPO, and model-free PPO).

Thorough and fair ablation study: each component (KL regularization, sample reuse, clipping) is isolated, and the authors proactively address a potential fairness concern by showing SAPO does not benefit from RPO's exponential learning rate schedule or 32 critic updates (Appendix C.3).

Good reproducibility: hyperparameters, architectures, environment counts, and the basis on official public repositories are documented in detail (Appendix A, C); the method builds on open-source codebases.
weaknesses: Theoretical treatment is informal: the connection between RPG and the surrogate objective (Section 4, Appendix D) is presented as a derivation of Monte Carlo estimators rather than a formal theorem with assumptions and error/bias analysis. In particular, the argument that the off-policy estimate is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the surrogate gradient deserves more scrutiny, since the reparameterization path includes dynamics Jacobians through a trajectory generated by the old policy, and the importance ratio only corrects the action probability term.

Empirical margins over SAPO are modest on several tasks: in Hopper (5480.85 vs 5478.12) and Hand Reorient (230.89 vs 225.23), the differences are well within reported standard deviations, so the claim of 'consistently achieves SOTA performance across all tasks' is somewhat overstated; the decisive wins are in Anymal and Humanoid.

Ablations are conducted only in the Humanoid environment; component-level conclusions (e.g., necessity of KL regularization and clipping) would be more convincing if validated on additional tasks, especially the manipulation task where dynamics and stability characteristics differ.

No analysis of computational cost: sample reuse (5 policy epochs and 32 critic epochs vs 16 for baselines) increases per-sample compute, and there is no wall-clock time comparison, which matters for assessing practical value relative to SHAC/SAPO's single-epoch design.

Limitations discussion is minimal: apart from mentioning sim-to-real transfer as future work, the paper does not discuss limitations such as reliance on differentiable dynamics (stiffness/contact issues), applicability to learned world models where gradients may be biased, or sensitivity to the many RPO-specific hyperparameters (c_low, c_high, lambda_KL, lambda_clip, entropy coefficients) that vary per task in Table 6.

Some implementation details are ad hoc and only empirically justified, e.g., not discounting explicitly computed entropy gradients, and hand-tuned per-task KL/entropy coefficients, raising questions about tuning burden versus baselines.

strengths: The paper establishes a clear and useful connection between the PPO-style surrogate objective and reparameterization policy gradients, and provides a formal proof (Proposition 1 in Appendix D) that the importance-weighted off-policy reparameterization gradient is unbiased, including a careful change-of-variables argument for the regenerated noise.

The proposed method is well-motivated: the motivating experiment (Figure 1) convincingly shows that SOTA RPG methods (SAPO) suffer KL spikes and performance collapses, and the three proposed mechanisms (surrogate optimization via RPG, asymmetric importance-ratio clipping, KL regularization) directly target this instability.

The evaluation is comparatively strong for this area: five tasks across two differentiable simulators, 24 effective runs per experiment (12 seeds × 2 simulator runs), multiple strong baselines (SAPO, SHAC, PPO, and an improved GI-PPO), and both deterministic and stochastic evaluation protocols.

The ablation study (Section 5.3, Appendix E) directly tests each of the three claimed components, and the extended ablation applying RPO's learning-rate schedule and critic iterations to SAPO addresses the plausible confound that gains come from hyperparameter tuning rather than the algorithmic design.
Reproducibility is well handled: complete hyperparameter tables (Tables 3–6) shared across baselines, architecture details, environment/reward details, and a statement of LLM usage.
weaknesses: There is a tension between the theory and the actual algorithm: Proposition 1 proves unbiasedness of the importance-weighted gradient, but the deployed estimator (Eq. 10) zeroes gradients outside the clipping range and weights them by ρ(θ), so the actual update is biased and no longer the gradient of the stated clipped surrogate objective. This bias, analogous to (but different from) PPO's, is never analyzed or even acknowledged, which weakens the paper's central theoretical narrative.

The novelty of the core connection is moderate: rewriting the surrogate objective in reparameterized form via the law of the unconscious statistician (Eq. 6) is fairly direct, and the off-policy estimator is essentially standard importance sampling applied to cached reparameterization action-gradients. The contribution is more an empirical algorithm design than a deep theoretical insight.

Ablations are performed only on Humanoid, and the final-performance differences are small relative to standard deviations (e.g., no-KL 8869 vs. RPO 8958, no-clipping 8818 vs. 8958), so the necessity of each component rests mostly on qualitative training-curve stability rather than statistically clear final-performance gaps.

Practical costs are under-discussed: caching action-gradients for every timestep of every trajectory and regenerating actions with an inverse transform across M epochs has nontrivial memory and compute overhead; no wall-clock or memory comparison against single-update baselines (SHAC/SAPO) is provided, so 'sample efficiency' claims ignore the extra per-sample compute.

The variance properties of the off-policy estimator (importance ratios multiplying potentially large BPTT action-gradients) are not analyzed, even though variance/stability is the paper's central concern; a variance analysis or empirical variance measurements would strengthen the claims.
The asymmetric clipping constants c_low/c_high and the KL/entropy coefficients appear hand-tuned per environment (Table 5) with no sensitivity analysis, raising robustness questions for new tasks.

Minor presentation issues: typos (e.g., 'optimizing a its surrogate objective' in Section 1), and the limitation discussion is brief, limited to a one-line mention of sim-to-real transfer in the conclusion.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: RPG-based methods (SHAC, SAPO) suffer from instability and cannot reuse samples, and the motivating Figure 1 (KL spikes correlating with performance drops in SAPO) provides concrete evidence for the claimed failure mode.

The core idea is clean and clearly presented: rewriting the PPO-style surrogate objective in reparameterization form (Eq. 6-7), caching action-gradients from a single BPTT pass, and reusing them with importance weighting across multiple update epochs. The unbiasedness of the off-policy estimator (Proposition 1) is proven correctly via a change-of-variables argument, including the subtlety of the regenerated noise distribution.

The evaluation is relatively thorough for this subfield: 12 seeds (24 effective runs) per experiment, two differentiable simulators, five tasks including a manipulation task, both deterministic and stochastic evaluation protocols, and hyperparameters largely shared across algorithms to isolate the algorithmic contribution.

The authors proactively address a potential confound in Appendix E by giving SAPO the same exponential LR schedule and 32 critic iterations, showing RPO's gains persist, and the ablations (no-KL, M=2, no-clipping) in Section 5.3 support the claimed role of each component.

The clipped importance-ratio mechanism (Eq. 10) is a sensible adaptation for RPG, with a reasonable argument for why PPO's symmetric, advantage-sign-dependent clipping does not transfer directly (RPG does not push action log-likelihoods).
weaknesses: The central theoretical insight is thinner than claimed. Equation 6 follows directly from the law of the unconscious statistician, and Proposition 1 is a straightforward change-of-variables argument. 'A novel connection... largely unexplored and non-trivial' (Abstract, Sec. 4.1) overstates the technical depth; the interesting part is algorithmic engineering rather than theory.

There is a tension between the theoretical framing and the actual algorithm: Proposition 1 establishes unbiasedness for the unclipped estimator, but Eq. 10 zeroes gradients outside the clipping range, so the deployed updates are biased. No analysis of this bias, its magnitude, or its effect on convergence is given, yet the paper's narrative leans on the 'principled' connection.

The headline empirical gains are modest relative to reported variance. In Table 1, RPO beats SAPO by 5.0 on Hopper (5534 vs 5478, SAPO std 4.5 vs RPO std 224) and 5.0 on Hand Reorient (230 vs 225, std ~30); no statistical significance tests (e.g., IQM with bootstrap CIs or t-tests) are reported. Claims of 'consistently achieves SOTA performance across all tasks' are therefore weaker than presented.

The ablation study is confined to a single environment (Humanoid), and the deltas are small: no-KL reaches 8869 vs 8958 for full RPO, and no-clipping reaches 8818 — both within one standard deviation. The strong claims that 'KL regularization stabilizes policy training' and the clipping mechanism is crucial are supported by only one task and largely qualitative curve inspection.

RPO uses more computation per iteration than the closest baseline (32 critic epochs and 5 actor epochs vs. 16 and 1 for SAPO; Appendix Table 3). While Appendix E partially addresses this, a wall-clock or compute-matched comparison is absent, which matters because the paper's motivation is explicitly about utilizing 'computationally expensive gradients' efficiently.

Generality is limited: all results are on rigid-body simulators with differentiable dynamics; the introduction motivates RPG via learned world models, but no such experiment is included. Whether the method transfers to learned (model-biased) dynamics is untested.

Presentation has notable defects: typos ('optimizing a its surrogate objective', p.2), broken/missing repository URLs in Appendix A (blank spaces where links should be), Figure 1 is a single-seed comparison presented as evidence of a systematic phenomenon, and hyperparameter tables (e.g., 'max oorr') contain unexplained terminology.
A limitations section is essentially absent; ethical considerations are trivial here, but reproducibility would benefit from a stated code-release plan (none is mentioned).

strengths: The core insight is clean and genuinely useful: establishing that the reparameterization gradient of a PPO-like surrogate objective can be computed via BPTT with cached action-gradients, and that off-policy reuse requires regenerating noise via the inverse reparameterization transform plus importance weighting. Proposition 1 in Appendix D gives a correct-looking change-of-variables proof of unbiasedness for the off-policy estimator, which is the key technical enabler for stable sample reuse in RPG methods.

The proposed clipping mechanism (Eq. 10) is thoughtfully tailored to RPG: the authors correctly identify that RPG, unlike REINFORCE, does not modify action log-likelihoods, so PPO's symmetric sign-dependent clipping is inappropriate, motivating an asymmetric, advantage-sign-independent rule.

The experimental evaluation is reasonably rigorous: five continuous control tasks across two differentiable simulators, 12 seeds with 24 effective runs, both deterministic and stochastic evaluation protocols, and comparisons against four baselines including the strong recent SAPO and the closely related GI-PPO. Hyperparameters and architectures are documented in detail (Tables 3-6) and largely shared across methods, supporting fairness.

The extended ablation in Appendix E directly addresses a plausible confound (RPO's exponential LR schedule and 32 critic iterations) by transferring those settings to SAPO, and shows SAPO degrades under them—strengthening the attribution of gains to the core algorithmic mechanism.
Practical contribution of a single BPTT pass per trajectory serving multiple update epochs is attractive given the expense of differentiable-simulator backward passes.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution, while correct, is fairly thin: the connection in Eq. 6-7 follows rather directly from applying the reparameterization trick and differentiating under the integral, and Proposition 1 is a standard change-of-variables/importance-weighting argument. The main novelty is algorithmic assembly (surrogate objective + RPG + clipping + KL), which is a solid but incremental contribution. The paper repeatedly labels this connection 'novel' and 'non-trivial,' which somewhat overstates it.

The clipping mechanism (Eq. 10) deliberately zeroes gradient contributions outside the ratio range, introducing bias with no theoretical characterization (no bound on bias magnitude, no discussion of how it interacts with the unbiased off-policy estimator of Proposition 1). The KL term is likewise added on heuristic grounds ('clipping alone is insufficient'). These design choices are pragmatic but under-theorized.

The ablation study is confined to a single environment (Humanoid) and the reported final-performance differences are small relative to standard deviations (e.g., RPO 8958±374 vs. no-KL 8869±431, M=2 8460±430), so claims like 'significantly less sample-efficient' are not clearly supported by the quantitative ablation table; component contributions may be marginal.

The evaluation suite is narrow (four DFlex locomotion tasks plus one manipulation task), all in simulation with privileged differentiable dynamics. There is no evidence on learned world models (despite RPG's motivation citing them), no higher-dimensional contact-rich tasks, and no sim-to-real experiments; generalization beyond DFlex-style simulators is unknown.

Reproducibility would benefit from an explicit code release statement; the paper relies on existing repositories (SAPO, AHAC, Rewarped) but no artifact is mentioned. Additionally, the memory footprint of caching per-action gradients (∇aR(τ) for every action in every trajectory) and its scaling with horizon/action dimension are never discussed.

Presentation has rough edges: several typos (e.g., 'optimizing a its surrogate objective'), a mismatch between the described symmetric clipping range '1 − c_low ≤ ρ ≤ 1 + c_high' and the described asymmetric motivation, Figure 1's axes are hard to read, and 'SOTA performance across all tasks' in Table 1 rests on differences that are within or near one standard deviation on several tasks (e.g., Hopper, Hand Reorient).
